:::{#exm-induction-sum}
#### Sum of the first $n$ natural numbers

For every $n \in \Nat$,

$$
\sumin i = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}.
$$

For example, with $n = 3$,
$1 + 2 + 3 = 6$ and $\frac{3 \cdot 4}{2} = 6$.
To prove the equation for every $n$,
let $P(n)$ be the equation and use @def-proof-by-induction with $n_0 = 1$.

**Base case, $n = 1$.**
The sum has one term:

$$
\ba
\sumto{i}{1} i
&= 1
&& \text{(definition of a sum)}
\ea
$$

and the right side is

$$
\ba
\frac{1\,(1+1)}{2}
&= \frac{1 \cdot 2}{2}
&& \text{(} 1 + 1 = 2 \text{)}
\\
&= \frac{2}{2}
&& \text{(} 1 \cdot 2 = 2 \text{)}
\\
&= 1.
&& \text{(} \tfrac{2}{2} = 1 \text{)}
\ea
$$

So $P(1)$ holds.

**Inductive step.**
Let $n \ge 2$, and suppose $P(n - 1)$ holds:

$$
\sumto{i}{n-1} i = \frac{(n-1)\,\paren{(n-1)+1}}{2}.
$$

Then

$$
\ba
\sumin i
&= 1 + 2 + \cdots + (n-1) + n
&& \text{(definition of a sum)}
\\
&= \paren{1 + 2 + \cdots + (n-1)} + n
&& \text{(associative law)}
\\
&= \sumto{i}{n-1} i + n
&& \text{(definition of a sum)}
\\
&= \frac{(n-1)\,\paren{(n-1)+1}}{2} + n
&& \text{(induction hypothesis)}
\\
&= \frac{(n-1)\,n}{2} + n
&& \text{(} (n-1) + 1 = n \text{)}
\\
&= \frac{(n-1)\,n}{2} + \frac{2n}{2}
&& \text{(} n = \tfrac{2n}{2} \text{)}
\\
&= \frac{(n-1)\,n + 2n}{2}
&& \text{(common denominator)}
\\
&= \frac{\paren{(n-1) + 2}\,n}{2}
&& \text{(distributive law)}
\\
&= \frac{(n+1)\,n}{2}
&& \text{(} (n-1) + 2 = n + 1 \text{)}
\\
&= \frac{n(n+1)}{2},
&& \text{(commutative law)}
\ea
$$

which is $P(n)$.
By @def-proof-by-induction,
the equation holds for every $n \in \Nat$.

:::
